title: Refuge in fear
hookLine: a kid in a thunderstorm runs down the hall; Shantideva, afraid, runs to a protector too
tomorrow: why not fix it later? Shantideva has a reason.

cards: Thunder at three in the morning, and a small kid sits bolt upright. She doesn't check the weather app. She doesn't reason about how lightning works.

She runs down the dark hall to the room where someone bigger is sleeping, and climbs in. Grown-ups have their own versions: the call to one particular friend, the place we drive to when things fall apart.
So, one question for today: when Shantideva gets scared, where does he run?

teach.h: AFRAID, LIKE A PRISONER LED AWAY.
teach.b: Halfway through chapter two, Shantideva looks at the harm he's done and gets frightened, like a prisoner being led away. So he does what the kid does.

He says that today he goes for refuge to the Buddhas, the mighty protectors of the world, who work to shield everyone. He goes for refuge to the teaching they found, and to the community of bodhisattvas.
Refuge, in Buddhism, has this shape: the Buddha, the dharma, the sangha. A teacher who woke up, the teaching, and the people walking it. He doesn't pretend not to be afraid.
He names it, then names where he's going. Neighbors know this movement well.

teach.h: GOD IS OUR REFUGE AND STRENGTH.
teach.b: In the Psalms, a Jewish and Christian book of songs, the King James English says: "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." Shared ground: fear is not the end of the sentence.
In both, someone afraid says out loud where they're turning, and turns. One honest difference: the psalm's refuge is God, the one Creator, and its comfort is trust in him.
Shantideva's refuge is in the Buddhas, the teaching and the community, and no creator is being addressed.
Two different shelters, and the same run down the hall.

how: Buddhists across schools recite going for refuge to the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha, often three times, at the start of chanting or practice; Mahayana Buddhists also turn to bodhisattvas as protectors.

o: naming your fear, then turning toward a protector
a safe house where monks hide during a war
running away from problems until they disappear

games.q: refuge, two ways — tap the pairs.
p: God is our refuge and strength

s: Shantideva says a real practitioner never feels afraid
he says he's frightened, like a prisoner led away, and then names where he turns.
Buddhist refuge is in the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha
a teacher who woke up, the teaching, and the community; Shantideva also names the bodhisattvas.
the psalm and Shantideva mean the same thing by refuge
both turn toward a protector when afraid, but the psalm's refuge is God, the Creator; Shantideva's is the Three Jewels.

games.q: you're scared about a test result coming tomorrow. by Shantideva's verses, what's the first move?
o: pretend you're fine, so the fear can't get any bigger.
name the fear plainly, then name where you'll turn: a person, a teaching, a practice.
search for every possible outcome until you feel ready.
games.why: Shantideva doesn't hide the fear. he names it, then says out loud where he's going for refuge.

practice: Sit up and rest one hand flat on your chest. Quietly name one fear you're carrying, in a few plain words. Then name one refuge you could turn to: a person, a teaching, a practice, a place.
Keep your hand there and let both names rest under it.

wordCard.voice: Refuge in fear: what Shantideva does when he's frightened. He names the fear, and turns toward the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha.

orig.note: Sanskrit: shelter, refuge, protection. In Pali the same word is sarana.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: a protector, and the courage it takes to run toward one. Seven days into the poem.

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 2.26 and 2.44-2.48 (going for refuge to the Buddhas, the dharma and the bodhisattvas; afraid, like one led to punishment)

sources.q: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
